title: Job 11:1–12
context: Zophar the Naamathite speaks for the first time. He rebukes Job’s many words, accuses him of claiming purity, and asserts that God exacts of him less than his iniquity deserves. He then speaks truly of God’s unsearchable wisdom, but uses that truth to press guilt on Job. Zophar’s words are a friend’s accusation, not the book’s endorsed doctrine; the prologue calls Job blameless (1:8), and in 42:7 the LORD says the friends have not spoken rightly of him. Both traditions read the passage as shared ground about God’s greatness and the danger of misapplied truth.

verses.arminianNotes:
Zophar the Naamathite answers, beginning his first speech. A third friend speaks.

Arminian readers note that Zophar’s words are a friend’s response, to be weighed in light of the book’s later verdict.
verses.reformedNotes:
In 42:7 the LORD says the friends “have not spoken of me the thing that is right, as my servant Job has.”

Reformed readers likewise read Zophar as a speaker within the drama, not the book’s voice. Both traditions read this as shared ground.

verses.text: “Shouldn’t the multitude of words be answered? Should a man full of talk be justified?
verses.arminianNotes:
Zophar asks whether so many words should go unanswered, and whether a talkative man should be vindicated. He opens with rebuke.

Arminian readers see Zophar dismissing Job’s lament as mere talk rather than hearing his pain.
verses.reformedNotes:
Zophar’s opening is often read as sharper than the earlier friends’, and he treats Job’s speech as a claim to be refuted.

Reformed readers see a friend who fails to listen. Both traditions read this as shared ground about the danger of answering grief with accusation.

verses.text: Should your boastings make men hold their peace? When you mock, will no man make you ashamed?
verses.arminianNotes:
Zophar asks whether Job’s boasting should silence others, and whether no one should shame him when he mocks. He accuses Job.

Arminian readers see a misreading of Job’s honest lament as arrogance, a judgment the book does not share.
verses.reformedNotes:
Zophar treats Job’s complaint as mockery of God.

Reformed readers see how quickly suffering can be misjudged by onlookers. Both traditions read this as shared ground, reporting Zophar’s accusation without adopting it, in light of the LORD’s later word in 42:7.

verses.text: For you say, ‘My doctrine is pure. I am clean in your eyes.’
verses.arminianNotes:
Zophar summarizes Job as saying his doctrine is pure and he is clean in God’s eyes. He condenses Job’s position.

Arminian readers note that Job has claimed integrity, not sinless perfection, so the summary is unfair.
verses.reformedNotes:
Zophar’s quotation is his own paraphrase and simplifies Job’s more complex words.

Reformed readers see a friend arguing against a position Job has not quite taken. Both traditions read this as shared ground about the danger of misrepresenting a sufferer.

verses.text: But oh that God would speak, and open his lips against you,
verses.arminianNotes:
Zophar wishes that God would speak and open his lips against Job. He expects God to side with him.

Arminian readers note the irony: God will speak (38:1), but his verdict will rebuke the friends (42:7).
verses.reformedNotes:
Zophar is confident he knows what God would say.

Reformed readers see presumption in claiming to speak for God. Both traditions read this as shared ground and let the book’s ending answer Zophar’s wish without overpressing it.

verses.text: that he would show you the secrets of wisdom! For true wisdom has two sides. Know therefore that God exacts of you less than your iniquity deserves.
verses.arminianNotes:
Zophar wishes God would show Job wisdom’s secrets and declares that God exacts of Job less than his iniquity deserves. The charge is severe.

Arminian readers hear a friend’s accusation, not the book’s verdict.
verses.reformedNotes:
The phrase about wisdom having ‘two sides’ is obscure. The prologue calls Job blameless (1:8), and 42:7 rebukes the friends.

Reformed readers likewise see a true principle misapplied to Job. Both traditions read this as shared ground.

verses.text: “Can you fathom the mystery of God? Or can you probe the limits of the Almighty?
verses.arminianNotes:
Zophar asks whether Job can fathom God’s mystery or find the limits of the Almighty. The question is true in itself.

Arminian readers affirm that God is beyond full human understanding.
verses.reformedNotes:
Scripture elsewhere confesses God’s unsearchable wisdom (compare Romans 11:33). Zophar’s error lies in using this truth against Job.

Reformed readers likewise affirm God’s incomprehensibility. Both traditions read this as shared ground about God’s depth, while noting its misapplication here.

verses.text: They are high as heaven. What can you do? They are deeper than Sheol. What can you know?
verses.arminianNotes:
Zophar says God’s wisdom is higher than heaven and deeper than Sheol; what can Job do or know? The image is vast.

Arminian readers affirm the truth that God’s wisdom exceeds human reach.
verses.reformedNotes:
Zophar speaks rightly of God’s greatness, but uses it to silence Job’s question rather than comfort him.

Reformed readers see a true confession misused. Both traditions read this as shared ground about God’s wisdom and about the pastoral failure of using true words wrongly.

verses.text: Its measure is longer than the earth, and broader than the sea.
verses.arminianNotes:
Zophar says the measure of God’s wisdom is longer than the earth and broader than the sea. The description continues.

Arminian readers again affirm that God’s wisdom is immeasurable and beyond human comprehension.
verses.reformedNotes:
The imagery fills all dimensions: height, depth, length, and breadth.

Reformed readers see God’s infinite wisdom confessed. Both traditions read this as shared ground, while remembering that the speaker applies it to accuse Job, a use the book later rejects.

verses.text: If he passes by, or confines, or convenes a court, then who can oppose him?
verses.arminianNotes:
Zophar asks who can oppose God if he passes by, confines, or convenes a court. God’s power is unstoppable.

Arminian readers affirm God’s authority while noting Zophar uses it to press guilt on Job.
verses.reformedNotes:
The legal image answers Job’s own wish for a hearing (9:33), but Zophar assumes the outcome.

Reformed readers affirm God’s sovereign justice. Both traditions read this as shared ground about God’s power, misapplied by Zophar.

verses.text: For he knows false men. He sees iniquity also, even though he doesn’t consider it.
verses.arminianNotes:
Zophar says God knows false men and sees iniquity, even though he does not seem to consider it. God sees all.

Arminian readers affirm God’s perfect knowledge, which Job has not denied (10:4–7).
verses.reformedNotes:
The last phrase is difficult, and its sense is debated. Zophar implies that God has seen hidden sin in Job.

Reformed readers affirm God’s omniscience while rejecting Zophar’s inference about Job. Both traditions read this as shared ground.

verses.text: An empty-headed man becomes wise when a man is born as a wild donkey’s colt.
verses.arminianNotes:
Zophar says an empty-headed man will become wise when a wild donkey’s colt is born a man. The proverb is cutting.

Arminian readers see an insult aimed at Job rather than counsel offered in love.
verses.reformedNotes:
The saying is obscure and rendered variously; it seems to suggest that some people never learn, though its exact force is uncertain.

Reformed readers see harsh words that fail as comfort. Both traditions read this as shared ground and report the insult as Zophar’s.
